title: How to Build a Rule of Life
excerpt: A rule of life is not a list of religious obligations. It is a trellis. It is the structure that holds your soul in place long enough for something to grow on it.
body:
Most of us do not drift toward God by accident. We drift away. We mean to pray more, read more, rest more, love the people in our house better, and then a year passes and we are exactly where we were, only more tired. The problem is rarely desire. The problem is that desire alone has no shape, and a soul without shape takes the shape of whatever is loudest.

A rule of life is the shape. The word comes from the Latin *regula*, the same root as *trellis*. A trellis does not make a vine grow. It holds the vine up so it can grow toward the sun instead of collapsing in the dirt. That is what we are building here. Not a performance review for your spiritual life. A structure that holds you in place long enough for grace to do its slow work.

## Start with honesty, not ambition

The first mistake is to design the rule for the person you wish you were. That person can pray an hour at dawn, fast twice a week, and read theology by candlelight. That person does not exist, and building a rule for him only produces shame when you fail to be him by Thursday.

Start instead with the person you actually are. What does your week actually contain? Where are the gaps, the dead minutes, the commute, the lunch break, the hour after the kids go down? A rule that ignores your real life is not a rule. It is a fantasy you will abandon. Jesus met people in their real conditions, at wells and tables and tax booths, not in the lives they pretended to have.

## Name the practices across a few categories

A durable rule touches several areas of life rather than stacking everything onto one heroic morning. Think in categories. Prayer: when and how you will talk to God. Scripture: what you will read and how often. Worship: your commitment to a gathered church. Rest: a real Sabbath, a real day off. Relationships: who you will love on purpose. Work: how your labor becomes offering rather than idol. Body: sleep, food, movement, the physical container God gave you.

Under each, name one small concrete practice. Not five. One. "I will read one psalm at breakfast." "I will not look at my phone before I have prayed." "Sunday is off, no email." Specificity is the difference between a rule and a wish.

## Build it small enough to keep

The ancient monastics who gave us this tradition were not gentle with themselves, but they were realistic. A rule you keep at sixty percent will form you. A rule you keep at zero because it was too heavy will not. Err toward small. You can always add. It is far harder to recover from the discouragement of a rule that crushed you in week two.

I have done this badly more times than I want to admit. I built rules that were really just monuments to who I wanted people to think I was. They never lasted, because pride is a poor engine and it runs out of fuel by February. The rules that held were the embarrassingly modest ones.

## Write it down and put it where you will see it

An unwritten rule is a mood, and moods do not survive contact with a hard week. Write your rule on one page. Tape it inside a cabinet, set it as your lock screen, keep it in the front of your Bible. You are not writing a contract with God, who already loves you and is not keeping score. You are writing a reminder to yourself of the life you said you wanted when you were thinking clearly.

## Review it with the seasons, not the failures

A rule of life is not permanent. The season of a newborn is not the season of an empty nest. Plan to revisit the rule a few times a year, gently, asking what is forming you and what is just guilt taking up space. Drop what is dead. Keep what is alive. This is not laxity. It is the same wisdom that lets a gardener prune.

And when you break the rule, and you will, do not treat it as a verdict on your soul. Treat it as Tuesday. Begin again. The whole tradition of spiritual formation is the tradition of beginning again, ten thousand times, because the God we are forming our lives toward is the kind of God who keeps welcoming the one who comes back.

## This week

Take one sheet of paper. Write down three practices, one each in the categories of prayer, rest, and relationships, and make each one small enough that you are almost embarrassed by how easy it is. Put the page where you will see it tomorrow morning. Keep it for seven days before you change a single word.

The trellis does not have to be impressive. It only has to hold.
